Bank of America seals one of India’s largest 2026 office deals: 10.1 lakh sq ft GCC in Hyderabad’s Mindspace
Bank of America’s India arm (BA Continuum India) has leased 10,10,467 sq ft across 12 floors at Mindspace Cyberabad, Building No. 1, Madhapur, for a 12-year term. The lease commenced on 7 September 2026, with rent starting January 2027 at ₹82 per sq ft (≈₹8.28 crore monthly) and a total estimated rental outgo of ₹1,450 crore, plus a ₹49.72 crore security deposit and 15% escalation every three years (19 November 2026). 
Key takeaway: A single GCC commitment of over 1 million sq ft and ~₹1,450 crore in rentals underscores Hyderabad’s ability to attract mega BFSI captives—reinforcing the city’s position among India’s top GCC destinations and supporting Grade-A absorption in Madhapur-Gachibowli.
Impact analysis:
•  Direct demand boost for large-format office space; GCCs already account for ~52% of Mindspace REIT leasing (up from 48% two years earlier). 
•  Positive spillover to residential rents and land values in IT corridors as thousands of high-skilled jobs are consolidated.
•  Strengthens investor sentiment in commercial REITs and signals sustained infrastructure pull for further GCC expansions.

Nov 12 to Nov 16: the week the digital world blinked.

November is turning into a black month for cybersecurity, and this week was the proof 👇

📧 Nov 12: Microsoft 365 went down worldwide. Outlook, Teams, Copilot hit. Lasted nearly 24 hours. Downdetector logged about 138,000 Outlook reports at peak.

✈️ Nov 13: FAA stopped departures nationwide for more than four hours, the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. About 12,000 scheduled flights couldn't take off. 

Same day Workday went down, employees across some 11,500 businesses locked out.

🏦 Nov 16: Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and others reported online banking trouble. More than 4,700 Chase reports by early afternoon, BofA above 2,000, Wells Fargo above 1,000. Chase said it was a Chase-only issue, other banks were affected only through transactions with Chase.

None of these were confirmed cyberattacks. Microsoft says its outage was not linked to any cyberattack. The investigations are still ongoing, so we'll see.

My take: we spend so much time planning for attackers that we forget to plan for plain failure.

But look at the result... When one system fails, everything connected to it feels it.
Cybersecurity isn't only about stopping attackers. It's also about staying up when something breaks.

Useful global snapshot this week.

One item that stands out for South African firms: 

New Zealand regulators are already pressing financial institutions on AI-driven cyber risks and whether their arrangements are keeping pace with the technology.

We do not yet have a dedicated AI law here, but POPIA and existing governance expectations still apply. 

The firms that treat AI risk as a current governance issue, rather than a future one, will be better positioned.

Banks are now deciding what a customer's AI agent is allowed to do.

In a Dallas Fed survey of 70 bankers, 11.4% said their institution had already restricted AI agents in online banking, and 22.9% plan to within 6 months. JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Schwab have said they won't let agents move customer money. 

On Monday, Fed Governor Michael Barr warned that agents shifting deposits on their own could speed up bank runs.

Blocking is the easy response. Coinbase went the other way last week with limits the agent can't override: a per-trade cap, a 24-hour cap and an auto-stop if the portfolio falls past a level the customer picks.

India may solve this at the rail level. Reuters reported in September that NPCI is designing a protocol that lets AI agents make small UPI payments within limits the account holder sets, building on UPI Circle and Reserve Pay. If that works, every bank and app on UPI gets the same permission model.

I expect customers to delegate more where those limits are easy to set and hard to break.

What Each Investment Bank Is Making From the Record-Breaking Anthropic IPO 🤯🏦

Anthropic is paying $550M in underwriting fees across 22 banks on its IPO, according to its final SEC prospectus.

The split follows each bank's share allocation in the syndicate.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were each allocated 20.5% of the shares, worth roughly $113M apiece. Together they take a whopping 41% of the pool.

J.P. Morgan and Citi come next at 10% each, or about $55M.

Barclays and Wells Fargo hold 7% each, or about $39M.

Bank of America, Deutsche Bank, RBC and UBS each have 3%, or roughly $16.5M.

Mizuho and MUFG sit at 2% each, about $11M.

The other 10 banks hold between 0.5% and 1.3%, collecting $3M to $7M each.

The $550M pool works out to about 0.68% of the $81.3B raise, which beats SpaceX's $75B as the largest IPO in history. 

The fee pool is also $50M bigger than the $500M banks earned on SpaceX, taking combined fees from the two deals past $1B.

Kerching.

Your bank just updated its terms to protect itself from your AI assistant.

Citi changed its customer agreement this week. If you connect a third-party AI tool to your account, you are responsible for everything it does. Even if it gets hacked. Even if it leaks your credentials. JPMorgan and Bank of America made the same change last month. PNC did the same this week.

One detail worth sitting with: Anthropic's own finance tool is read-only. It cannot move your money at all.

The banks read this moment early. People are about to hand account access to AI tools at scale, and the banks have already decided who pays when it goes wrong.

If your business finances run through software, treat AI account access like handing a new hire the company card. Read-only until it earns trust. One named owner for every connection. A log of everything it touches. Your bank has already told you it will not cover the mistake.

10–50% productivity gains. AI in banking has moved past pilots and into results.

A new report in ET CIO says banks are seeing 10–50% productivity improvements from AI in customer service and operations. Those are the two areas where banks spend the most effort, and where customers notice delays the most.
Source: Revolutionary Gains: Banks Boost Productivity by Up to 50% with AI Innovations, ETCIO https://lnkd.in/gjmYST5d

The pattern shows up across the industry:
🔹 At Bank of America, more than 90% of employees use its internal assistant, which has cut IT service desk calls by over 50%.
🔹 At Citi, nearly 9 out of 10 employees are using the bank's AI tools.
🔹 Bank leaders expect productivity in operations roles to rise 40–50% as more routine work is automated.

The real win isn't headcount. It's capacity. AI handles the routine queries, reconciliations and document checks, so people can spend their time on the cases that need judgment and empathy.

Where Salesforce fits in
Salesforce has been one of the companies turning this from an idea into a working product:
✅ Agentforce for Financial Services: ready-made AI agents for bankers, advisors and loan officers that handle meeting prep, follow-ups and service requests.
✅ AI and people on one platform: the agents run inside Financial Services Cloud, so AI and human staff work from the same customer record.
✅ Measured results: Absa Relationship Banking reported issues being resolved 88% faster.

Where it can add even more value:
1️⃣ Clean, unified customer data. AI is only as good as the data behind it. Bringing together data scattered across older core banking systems is where most banks are still stuck.
2️⃣ Getting past the pilot. Many AI projects stall after the proof-of-concept stage. Pre-built banking workflows and built-in compliance controls can help them scale.
3️⃣ Room for mid-sized banks. Regional and co-operative banks, including many in India, can offer always-on service without the IT budgets of the biggest banks.
4️⃣ Smooth handoffs to people. AI should resolve the simple 70% and pass the complex 30% to a person, with full context, so the customer never has to repeat themselves.

Productivity is the headline today. Better customer experience is the real story.

Global Capital Takes Control: A $20 Billion Strategic Bet on India’s Financial Sector

India’s financial sector is witnessing a major shift in foreign investment. In 2025–26, global banks, sovereign funds and private equity investors committed approximately $18 billion in disclosed deals and over $20 billion including undisclosed transactions.

Unlike earlier portfolio investments, this wave increasingly involves strategic stakes, board representation, partnerships and controlling acquisitions.

Major transactions

BANKING SECTOR

1. IDBI Bank – Fairfax (Canada): ~$6.3 billion for 60.72%, a landmark privatisation deal.
2. RBL Bank – Emirates NBD (UAE): ~$2.75 billion for 60% control.
3. Yes Bank – SMBC (Japan): $1.6 billion+ for 24.2%, a major Japanese banking investment.
4. IDFC First Bank – Warburg Pincus & ADIA: ~$900 million for ~10%, providing growth capital.
5. Federal Bank – Blackstone (US): ~$705 million for 9.9%, with board representation.

NBFCs & FINANCIAL SERVICES

6. Shriram Finance – MUFG (Japan): ~$4.4 billion for 20%, a landmark NBFC investment.
7. IIFL Finance – Blackstone (US): ~$535 million for ~16%, strengthening its capital base.
8. Manappuram Finance – Bain Capital (US): ~$510 million for up to 41.7%, bringing strategic joint control.
9. Godrej Capital – Temasek (Singapore): ~$267 million for ~20%, supporting its ₹1 lakh crore AUM ambition by 2031.
10. Jio Financial – Bank of America (US): Undisclosed investment; 49.9% lending JV.
11. Avendus Capital – Mizuho (Japan): Undisclosed value; acquisition of KKR’s stake, giving Mizuho majority ownership.

What is driving this investment?

Three factors stand out:

* Credit potential: India’s credit-to-GDP is ~50%, while the MSME credit gap is estimated at ₹30 lakh crore.
* Stronger lenders: Improved asset quality, recoveries and underwriting discipline.
* Regulatory openness: Greater acceptance of credible, long-term foreign strategic investors.

A counter-trend is Deutsche Bank’s proposed sale of its Indian retail and wealth business to Kotak Mahindra Bank, reflecting a parallel consolidation of foreign banking operations.

The larger message

Of the ~$18 billion disclosed, banks account for ~$12.3 billion and NBFCs/financial services ~$5.7 billion.

This is more than an FDI story. Global capital is moving beyond passive investment to influence ownership, governance and the institutions financing India’s growth.

India’s next financial growth cycle may be shaped as much by global balance sheets, strategic partnerships and international banking expertise as by domestic capital.

Major U.S. Banks Face Widespread Disruptions: A Wake-Up Call for Digital Banking

When customers cannot access their money, even a short banking disruption can create a major loss of confidence.

Reports of widespread service disruptions involving major U.S. banks and financial services providers have put digital banking reliability back in the spotlight. Names shown include Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi, Capital One, U.S. Bank, and services such as Zelle.

The bigger issue goes beyond temporary login or transaction problems. Modern businesses and consumers depend on uninterrupted access to payments, transfers, and account information.

For financial institutions, this highlights three priorities:

Resilient infrastructure: 

Systems must be designed to handle failures without bringing essential services to a halt.

Clear communication: 

Customers need timely, transparent updates when services are affected.

Reliable recovery: 

Banks should have tested backup systems and incident-response plans to restore services quickly.

As digital banking becomes the default, reliability is no longer just a technical requirement. It is a core part of customer trust and financial stability.

A question for banking and fintech leaders: Is the industry investing enough in infrastructure resilience, or are we still treating reliability as an afterthought?

My take: AI contracts are moving from “who” to “who pays”.

This week TechCrunch reported that Citi updated its user agreement. A Citi spokesperson says “customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” TechCrunch also reported that PNC, JPMorgan and Bank of America have made similar moves.

That’s a consumer story. But I think it’s a preview of every services contract we’ll sign in the next few years.

Here’s how I see the shift.

Old way: we priced the people. Headcount, rate card, SLA. If something broke, the contract already said whose team owned the fix.
AI way: an agent does part of the work, and in my view the hard question becomes who carries the risk when it gets it wrong. The vendor’s agent? The client’s agent? A third-party tool someone plugged in?

Gartner’s Tom Coshow put it well in CIO Dive: “If the vendor isn’t taking on the risk, why are you bothering with outcome-based pricing?”

In my experience running delivery and migration programmes, scope rarely causes the big fights. Unclear ownership does. I’ve seen more time lost arguing “whose problem is this” than fixing the actual issue.

So my simple before/after test for any AI-heavy deal:
Before: “How many people, at what rate?”
After: “When the agent makes a bad call at 2am, whose name is on the fix, and who absorbs the cost?”

Your AI agent gets hacked. Your bank says: not our problem.

This week, Citi updated its Online User Agreement with a new section on third-party AI agents. The terms are blunt: if you give an AI agent access to your bank account, you are responsible for everything it does — including what a hacker does with it if the agent leaks your credentials or gets compromised.

PNC changed its terms the same day. Citizens emailed customers with a similar warning this week. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced the same policy in October. That is five major US banks, all telling customers the same thing: the agent's actions are yours.

And here is the detail that tells you everything about where the power sits: Citi's own AI agents are exempt. Use the bank's agent, no added liability. Use your own, and the loss is yours.

Why this matters for anyone building with agents: an agent holding your bank login is a credential with a wallet attached. There is no spending limit in the terms, no kill switch, no approval step — just a login handed to software that can be prompt-injected, phished, or breached. The banks have now priced that risk. It is yours.

That is exactly the gap RaksHex closes: ALLOW or DENY before anything executes — budgets and kill switches on every call, and credentials issued just-in-time, scoped to one task, so a compromised agent has nothing to spend and nothing to leak.

One honest caveat: whether federal rules on unauthorized transfers would still protect a customer in a real dispute is unresolved — no regulator or court has decided yet. The banks' terms say one thing; the law has not answered.
